note: The real-history spine, v2 (M16): 1578 curated anchor events, antiquity to the present, with themes, multi-region reach, magnitude, and attractor strength. Hand-authored context for the record rail, retrieval, and convergence detection; never generated content. Assembled by scripts/build-baseline.mjs.

anchors.title: Maize is fully domesticated in Mesoamerica
anchors.summary: Millennia of selection turn a wild grass into the crop that will feed hemispheric civilizations.

anchors.title: Cuneiform writing emerges at Uruk
anchors.summary: Temple accountants in Sumer press marks into clay; administration becomes memory that outlives the administrator.

anchors.title: The small tool tradition spreads across Australia
anchors.summary: Backed blades and hafted points appear from coast to coast, the widest technological change on the continent since people first arrived.

anchors.title: Upper and Lower Egypt are unified under one crown
anchors.summary: A single kingdom now runs seven hundred miles of the Nile, and its granaries, taxes, and scribes are organized around one river's flood.

anchors.title: Platform mounds rise at Aspero on the Peruvian coast
anchors.summary: Fishing communities working cotton nets and using no pottery pile up some of the earliest monumental architecture in the Americas.

anchors.title: Bantu-speaking farmers begin moving south
anchors.summary: From the Cameroon grasslands, villages carrying yams, goats, and later iron start a dispersal that will fill half of Africa with related languages.

anchors.title: Corded Ware herders carry steppe ancestry into Europe
anchors.summary: Migrants out of the Pontic steppe replace much of central Europe's ancestry within a few generations and bring the languages most Europeans still speak.

anchors.title: Sumer's cities enter the Early Dynastic period
anchors.summary: Uruk, Ur, Kish, and Lagash wall themselves, seat kings beside their temples, and begin centuries of quarrelling over land and water.

anchors.title: Early Harappan towns take shape along the Indus
anchors.summary: Kot Diji and its neighbours adopt mudbrick platforms, standardized pottery, and perimeter walls, the rehearsal for the cities that follow.

anchors.title: Liangzhu's walled city works jade at scale
anchors.summary: In the Yangtze delta a rice-farming society builds dams and moats and buries its elite with jade insignia cut by full-time specialists.

anchors.title: Malta's builders raise the Tarxien temples
anchors.summary: Islanders quarry and fit multi-ton limestone slabs into walled sanctuaries centuries before anything comparable is attempted on the mainland.

anchors.title: Egyptian ships fetch cedar from Byblos
anchors.summary: A land without tall timber buys Lebanese cedar by the shipload for hulls, roof beams, and coffins, and the Levantine port grows rich on the traffic.

anchors.title: Cycladic sculptors carve the folded-arm figures
anchors.summary: Island workshops turn marble into pale, nearly abstract human forms that travel the Aegean as grave goods and as trade.

anchors.title: Djoser's step pyramid rises at Saqqara
anchors.summary: Imhotep stacks six stone terraces into the first monumental building in dressed stone, and Egyptian kingship acquires its architecture.

anchors.title: Caral builds plazas in the Supe valley
anchors.summary: Irrigated cotton fields and sunken plazas support an inland city with no pottery, no writing, and no fortifications, the oldest known urban center in the Americas.

anchors.title: The Mature Harappan phase begins
anchors.summary: Indus cities standardize brick proportions, weights, and street grids across half a million square miles, with no palaces or royal tombs anywhere in evidence.

anchors.title: The Great Pyramid rises at Giza
anchors.summary: Khufu's builders organize tens of thousands of laborers and rations on a scale no state had managed before.

anchors.title: Troy's second citadel fortifies the strait
anchors.summary: A small hilltop town at the mouth of the Dardanelles accumulates gold, bronze, and walls by taxing traffic between the Aegean and the Black Sea.

anchors.title: Mohenjo-daro lays out its grid and Great Bath
anchors.summary: Baked-brick drains run beneath gridded streets and a sealed public tank sits on the citadel, sanitation on a scale rare anywhere before Rome.

anchors.title: The Sahara completes its drying
anchors.summary: Lakes and grazing land that had supported herders for millennia fail, pushing populations toward the Nile and splitting the continent with a desert.

anchors.title: Stonehenge's sarsen circle is raised
anchors.summary: Stones of twenty-five tons are hauled some twenty miles and jointed with carpentry techniques, the culmination of a thousand years of building on the site.

anchors.title: Tin bronze becomes the standard alloy
anchors.summary: Harder and easier to cast than arsenical copper, tin bronze forces every workshop in the Near East into long-distance dependence on scarce tin.

anchors.title: Lagash and Umma fight over a boundary canal
anchors.summary: Eannatum's victory stele is one of the earliest wars recorded in writing, complete with a count of the dead and the text of an oath.

anchors.title: Paleo-Inuit hunters spread across the Arctic
anchors.summary: A toolkit of tiny flaked blades carries people from Alaska to Greenland within a few centuries, the last great settlement of empty land in the north.

anchors.title: Kerma rises above the third cataract
anchors.summary: A Nubian kingdom takes control of the gold, ivory, and cattle routes south of Egypt and will hold them, on and off, for a thousand years.

anchors.title: Longshan towns wrap themselves in rammed earth
anchors.summary: Along the Yellow River hundreds of settlements raise pounded-earth walls and stratify their burials, the archaeology of chiefs before dynasties.

anchors.title: The Pyramid Texts are carved for Unas
anchors.summary: Spells meant to carry a dead king into the sky are cut into his burial chamber at Saqqara, the oldest substantial religious writing yet found.

anchors.title: Sargon founds the Akkadian empire
anchors.summary: The first durable multi-city empire yokes Sumer's rival temples to one crown and one road network.

anchors.title: Taosi walls a capital in the Shanxi basin
anchors.summary: A town of some three hundred hectares with an observatory platform and graded tombs marks north China's first city-scale hierarchy, and is violently sacked later.

anchors.title: Enheduanna signs her temple hymns at Ur
anchors.summary: Sargon's daughter, installed as high priestess, composes hymns in the first person and becomes the earliest author known anywhere by name.

anchors.title: Akkadian records name Meluhha as a trading partner
anchors.summary: Indus seals, carnelian beads, and a scribe titled interpreter of Meluhhan turn up in Mesopotamia, evidence of sea trade between two literate civilizations.

anchors.title: A two-century drought grips the northern world
anchors.summary: Sediment cores from Mesopotamia to the Indus record a sharp arid phase that coincides with the fall of Akkad and the fragmentation of Old Kingdom Egypt.

anchors.title: The domestic horse lineage spreads out of the steppe
anchors.summary: Ancient DNA traces nearly all later horses to one Volga-Don population whose descendants reach central Europe and Anatolia within a few centuries.

anchors.title: Egypt's Old Kingdom breaks apart
anchors.summary: Low Niles, a long reign's exhausted end, and provincial governors with their own troops leave Egypt divided between rival capitals for a century.

anchors.title: The Akkadian empire fragments
anchors.summary: The first territorial empire loses its provinces to drought, revolt, and Gutian raiding, and later scribes explain the fall as a god's punishment.

anchors.title: Ur-Nammu's code fixes penalties in silver
anchors.summary: The oldest surviving law code prices injuries in weighed silver rather than retaliation, centuries before Hammurabi's stele.

anchors.title: The Xia dynasty is traditionally founded
anchors.summary: Chinese tradition dates the first dynasty to Yu the Great's flood control; the archaeology of those centuries shows large walled centers but carries no name.

anchors.title: Mentuhotep II reunifies Egypt
anchors.summary: A Theban king ends the war between north and south and opens the Middle Kingdom, with quarry expeditions and frontier forts resuming within a decade.

anchors.title: Elam sacks Ur
anchors.summary: The Third Dynasty's accounting empire ends with its last king carried off, and Sumerian survives afterward only as a language of scribes and liturgy.

anchors.title: New drainage ditches are cut at Kuk
anchors.summary: Highland New Guinea gardeners extend a wetland field system already thousands of years old, farming bananas and taro with no imported crops at all.

anchors.title: Sintashta graves hold the first spoked-wheel chariots
anchors.summary: In the southern Urals, fortified villages bury paired horses with light two-wheeled vehicles, and within a few centuries chariots are fighting in Anatolia and Egypt.

anchors.title: The first palaces are built on Crete
anchors.summary: Knossos, Phaistos, and Malia each gather storage, workshops, and ritual into one complex, and Crete begins keeping accounts in a script of its own.

anchors.title: Erlitou lays out palace platforms
anchors.summary: On the Yellow River plain a planned center of rammed-earth compounds and the first Chinese bronze vessel foundries sets the model for dynastic capitals.

anchors.title: The Indus cities are abandoned
anchors.summary: Weakening monsoons and shifting rivers empty Mohenjo-daro and Harappa within a few generations, and their script goes out of use undeciphered.

anchors.title: Assyrian merchants keep books at Kanesh
anchors.summary: A trading colony in Anatolia leaves some twenty thousand tablets of loans, partnerships, and family quarrels, the earliest detailed record of private commerce.

anchors.title: Babylon becomes an Amorite kingdom
anchors.summary: Sumu-abum takes a minor town on the Euphrates and founds the dynasty whose sixth king, Hammurabi, will make its name a synonym for Mesopotamia.

anchors.title: Sinai miners scratch the first alphabet
anchors.summary: Semitic speakers borrow a handful of Egyptian signs for their sounds alone, cutting writing down to about two dozen letters and beginning nearly every alphabet in use today.

anchors.title: U-shaped ceremonial centers rise on the Peruvian coast
anchors.summary: Canal irrigation, pottery, and plazas framed by two arms of platform mounds organize whole valleys around shared ritual construction.

anchors.title: Linear A is written on Crete
anchors.summary: Minoan administrators drop their hieroglyphs for a syllabary used on inventories and offering tables, a script still unread because its language is unknown.

anchors.title: Hammurabi publishes his law code
anchors.summary: Babylon carves prices, wages, and penalties in stone, law as public infrastructure.

anchors.title: Crete rebuilds its palaces larger
anchors.summary: After destructions across the island, Knossos and its rivals rise again with light wells, frescoes, and deeper storerooms, and Minoan goods reach the whole Aegean.

anchors.title: Earthworks rise at Poverty Point
anchors.summary: Hunter-gatherers in the lower Mississippi valley move hundreds of thousands of cubic yards of soil into concentric ridges and mounds, without farming and without kings.

anchors.title: Hattusili I makes Hattusa the Hittite capital
anchors.summary: The Hittite kingdom settles behind Anatolian stone walls and begins raiding south into Syria, keeping its records in cuneiform but in its own language.

anchors.title: The Hyksos rule Egypt from Avaris
anchors.summary: Rulers of Levantine descent take the delta and govern as pharaohs, bringing the composite bow, the horse and chariot, and new bronze working with them.

anchors.title: Mycenae's shaft graves fill with gold
anchors.summary: Mainland Greek warlords are buried with imported gold, amber, and weapons, evidence of a new elite trading and raiding the length of the Aegean.

anchors.title: The Shang dynasty is founded
anchors.summary: A Yellow River state with chariots, walled capitals, and industrial bronze foundries begins the first Chinese dynasty attested by its own writing.

anchors.title: Thera erupts and buries Akrotiri
anchors.summary: One of the largest eruptions of the Holocene destroys a Cycladic port, drops ash across the eastern Mediterranean, and drives waves onto Crete's north coast.

anchors.title: Mursili I sacks Babylon
anchors.summary: A Hittite raid down the Euphrates ends Hammurabi's dynasty, and the Kassites inherit a Babylonia its conquerors never attempted to hold.

anchors.title: Ahmose expels the Hyksos
anchors.summary: Theban armies retake the delta and push into the Levant, opening a New Kingdom that garrisons foreign territory instead of merely trading with it.

anchors.title: Lapita pottery appears in the Bismarck Archipelago
anchors.summary: Austronesian voyagers arrive with outrigger canoes, pigs, and dentate-stamped pottery, and their descendants will cross open ocean to Fiji, Tonga, and Samoa.

anchors.title: The dingo reaches Australia
anchors.summary: A tame dog arrives with seafarers from island Southeast Asia and spreads across the mainland within centuries, the last major animal introduction before Europeans.

anchors.title: Indo-Aryan speakers enter the Punjab
anchors.summary: Herding clans from the steppe move into the northwest with horses, chariots, and the language that will become Sanskrit.

anchors.title: Building stops at Stonehenge
anchors.summary: The last pits are cut around the sarsen circle, and the monument passes from a fifteen-century construction site to an inherited ruin.

anchors.title: Hatshepsut is crowned king of Egypt
anchors.summary: Thutmose III's regent takes the full royal titulary, rules for two decades, and pays for temples and southern trading voyages out of Nubian gold.

anchors.title: Thutmose III takes Megiddo
anchors.summary: Egypt's army risks a narrow pass, scatters a Canaanite coalition, and holds the town through a seven-month siege; the campaign is recorded step by step at Karnak.

anchors.title: Mycenaeans take over Knossos
anchors.summary: After the Cretan palaces burn, Greek-speaking administrators run Knossos, and the Aegean's trade and craft networks pass into mainland hands.

anchors.title: Linear B records Greek in palace accounts
anchors.summary: Mycenaean scribes adapt Cretan signs to tally rations, chariot wheels, and offerings, using writing for administration and for nothing else.

anchors.title: Sechín Alto dominates the Casma valley
anchors.summary: Andean builders raise the largest structure yet built anywhere in the Americas, a stone and clay platform facing a chain of sunken plazas.

anchors.title: Ugarit writes an alphabet in cuneiform
anchors.summary: Scribes in the Syrian port cut thirty wedge-shaped letters and teach them in a fixed order, leaving the oldest known alphabetic sequence.

anchors.title: Ashur-uballit I frees Assyria from Mitanni
anchors.summary: Assur stops paying tribute, writes to the pharaoh as a great king in his own right, and founds a Middle Assyrian state that expands for two centuries.

anchors.title: Akhenaten raises the Aten above Egypt's gods
anchors.summary: The pharaoh closes the old temples, moves the court to a new desert capital, and turns their revenue toward a single sun disc and toward himself.

anchors.title: The Amarna letters carry great-king diplomacy
anchors.summary: Clay tablets in Akkadian move marriage offers, gold demands, and vassal complaints between Egypt, Babylon, Hatti, Assyria, and Mitanni.

anchors.title: Suppiluliuma I builds the Hittite empire
anchors.summary: Hattusa's king breaks Mitanni and annexes northern Syria, making Anatolia one of the three powers the Near East has to negotiate with.

anchors.title: Tutankhamun restores the old cults
anchors.summary: A boy king's decree reopens Amun's temples, gives the priesthoods back their land and staff, and abandons his father's desert capital.

anchors.title: A loaded merchantman sinks off Uluburun
anchors.summary: Ten tons of Cypriot copper, a ton of tin, Canaanite jars, ebony, ivory, and Baltic amber go down in one hull, the Bronze Age trade system in cross section.

anchors.title: Cyprus supplies the age its copper
anchors.summary: Oxhide ingots cast near Enkomi turn up from Sardinia to Syria, tying one island's mines to every bronze workshop in the eastern Mediterranean.

anchors.title: The last Harappan towns are given up
anchors.summary: Village cultures replace the Indus cities' standard weights, seals, and drains, and the script falls out of use.

anchors.title: The Shang move their capital to Yin
anchors.summary: Anyang becomes a permanent royal seat with bronze foundries, chariot burials, and a divination archive that runs until the dynasty falls.

anchors.title: Urnfield cremation spreads across central Europe
anchors.summary: Communities from the Danube to the Rhine burn their dead and bury the ashes in pots, sharing a rite, sheet bronze work, and the slashing sword.

anchors.title: Egypt and Hatti fight to a draw at Kadesh
anchors.summary: Ramesses II marches into an ambush on the Orontes, extracts his army, and has the escape carved on temple walls as a personal victory.

anchors.title: Egypt and Hatti swear a written peace
anchors.summary: Silver tablets exchanged by Ramesses II and Hattusili III promise no invasion, mutual defense, and the return of fugitives, the oldest surviving international treaty.

anchors.title: Mycenae fortifies its citadel
anchors.summary: Cyclopean walls, a carved lion gate, and a stair down to a hidden cistern turn a palace hill into a stronghold built for a siege.

anchors.title: Shang diviners inscribe oracle bones
anchors.summary: Under Wu Ding, questions about harvests, childbirth, and campaigns are burned into ox shoulder blades and turtle shells, leaving China's earliest writing.

anchors.title: Hundreds die in battle in the Tollense valley
anchors.summary: Bones with embedded arrowheads and crushed skulls along a north German river record organized fighting on a scale not previously credited to Bronze Age Europe.

anchors.title: Merneptah's victory stele names Israel
anchors.summary: An Egyptian hymn listing beaten Libyans and Canaanite towns includes a people called Israel, the earliest known written mention of the name.

anchors.title: Cupisnique style spreads on Peru's north coast
anchors.summary: Adobe platforms, stirrup-spout bottles, and feline imagery link the coastal valleys and lay the groundwork for the Chavín horizon.

anchors.title: Miners cut salt inside the Hallstatt mountain
anchors.summary: Alpine shafts run hundreds of meters into rock salt, and the picks, packs, and clothing preserved there show a full-time industry supplying central Europe.

anchors.title: Olmec centers rise on the Gulf coast
anchors.summary: Mesoamerica's first monumental culture carves colossal heads and sets templates its successors inherit.

anchors.title: The Rigveda settles into fixed oral form
anchors.summary: Priestly families memorize a thousand hymns syllable by syllable and pass them on intact for centuries before anyone writes them down.

anchors.title: Bronze giants are buried at Sanxingdui
anchors.summary: A walled city in Sichuan casts masks, a tree of birds, and figures taller than men, then breaks them and buries them in pits, leaving no writing behind.

anchors.title: Ugarit burns and is not reoccupied
anchors.summary: The Syrian port's last letters report enemy ships off the coast; the city ends, and with it a school, an archive, and a trade in copper and grain.

anchors.title: Greek tradition dates the fall of Troy
anchors.summary: Later chronographers fix the sack at this year, giving the Greek cities a common heroic past to date their genealogies and colonies from.

anchors.title: Hattusa burns and Hittite rule ends
anchors.summary: The capital is stripped and fired, the royal line disappears, and Anatolian power breaks into small successor kingdoms in the southeast.

anchors.title: The palace at Pylos burns
anchors.summary: Fire bakes the clay tablets recording its last months, watchers posted to the coast among them, and Mycenaean palace administration ends with the building.

anchors.title: The Bronze Age system collapses
anchors.summary: Within a generation the palace economies of the eastern Mediterranean burn or starve; trade, literacy, and cities retreat for centuries.

anchors.title: Ramesses III turns back the Sea Peoples
anchors.summary: Egypt destroys a coalition's ships in the delta mouths and settles the survivors as garrison troops, an outcome carved at length on the walls of Medinet Habu.

anchors.title: Tomb workers strike at Deir el-Medina
anchors.summary: Late grain rations halt work on the royal tombs; the crews sit down behind the mortuary temples until they are paid, in the earliest recorded strike.

anchors.title: Tyre plants a colony at Gadir
anchors.summary: Phoenician traders settle the Atlantic side of Iberia to reach silver and tin, according to a tradition that dates the founding to this year.

anchors.title: Aramaean kingdoms form across Syria
anchors.summary: Pastoral clans occupy the ground between fallen empires, found states at Damascus and along the Euphrates, and spread a language that outlasts all of them.

anchors.title: Tin moves along the Atlantic seaways
anchors.summary: Ingots from southwest Britain travel by boat to Brittany and Iberia, binding the ocean coast into a single bronze economy.

anchors.title: Iron-working spreads through the Near East
anchors.summary: Cheap iron loosens the bronze monopolies; farming and war both change hands.

anchors.title: Lapita settlers reach Vanuatu and New Caledonia
anchors.summary: Canoe crews carrying pigs, taro, and pottery cross hundreds of kilometers of open water to island chains no one had lived on before.

anchors.title: Egypt divides between Tanis and Thebes
anchors.summary: The New Kingdom ends as Smendes takes the delta and the high priests of Amun hold the south, and a single Egyptian state does not return for centuries.

anchors.title: Camel caravans open the desert routes
anchors.summary: Loaded dromedaries cross the Arabian interior, and incense from the south reaches Levantine markets without following the coast.

anchors.title: Greek speakers settle the Anatolian coast
anchors.summary: Families from Attica and the Peloponnese cross the Aegean and found the Ionian cities, carrying their dialects, cults, and quarrels with them.

anchors.title: The Phoenician alphabet takes shape
anchors.summary: Twenty-two letters a merchant can learn replace scripts only scribes could master.

anchors.title: The Zhou claim the Mandate of Heaven
anchors.summary: A new dynasty justifies conquest with a theory of legitimacy that will govern Chinese politics for three millennia.

anchors.title: The Duke of Zhou puts down the eastern revolt
anchors.summary: A regent crushes a rising of Shang loyalists and royal kinsmen, then builds Chengzhou to garrison the conquered east.

anchors.title: The Zhou settle kinsmen in walled towns
anchors.summary: Relatives and allies receive titles and garrisons to hold the conquered east, creating the lineage states that will later fight each other for centuries.

anchors.title: Bantu-speaking farmers move east of the forest
anchors.summary: Cultivators carrying yams, oil palm, and pottery spread from the Cameroon grasslands toward the Great Lakes, beginning the continent's largest language spread.

anchors.title: Iron tools open the Ganges plain
anchors.summary: Axes and ploughshares cut monsoon forest that copper could not, and settlement moves east into the rice country that will hold most of India's people.

anchors.title: Polynesian navigators settle the remote Pacific
anchors.summary: Star paths and double-hulled canoes carry settlers across the largest ocean, island by island.

anchors.title: Tyre leads the Phoenician cities
anchors.summary: An island port with two harbors takes over eastern Mediterranean shipping, purple dye, and metal broking now that the palace empires are gone.

anchors.title: King Zhao's southern army is lost on the Han
anchors.summary: A Zhou expedition toward the middle Yangtze never returns, and the dynasty gives up pushing south for good.

anchors.title: The Kuru realm orders Vedic ritual
anchors.summary: Clans of the upper Ganges and Yamuna country merge into one dominant polity and arrange the hymns into a fixed sacrificial system run by a priestly hierarchy.

anchors.title: A rich burial is raised at Lefkandi
anchors.summary: A long apsidal building on Euboea covers a cremated man, a woman, and four horses with gold and an heirloom bronze urn, wealth the Greek dark age is not supposed to hold.

anchors.title: The Israelite kingdom splits in two
anchors.summary: Northern tribes refuse Rehoboam's demands for labor and tribute and crown their own king, leaving Israel and Judah as rival neighbors.

anchors.title: Adad-nirari II begins Assyria's recovery
anchors.summary: Yearly campaigns and permanent garrisons rebuild the state that will dominate the Near East for three centuries.

anchors.title: Aegean bards carry a Bronze Age past in verse
anchors.summary: Singers keep formulaic hexameter accounts of Mycenaean kings and a war at Troy, the tradition from which the Iliad and Odyssey are later fixed.

anchors.title: Anuradhapura grows into an iron-using town
anchors.summary: A settlement beside Sri Lanka's dry-zone rivers works iron, keeps cattle, and reaches town size centuries before its monasteries are built.

anchors.title: Chavín de Huántar becomes an Andean pilgrimage center
anchors.summary: A highland temple complex knits scattered valleys into one ritual and trade sphere.

anchors.title: La Venta becomes the Olmec center
anchors.summary: As San Lorenzo fades, an island in the Tabasco swamps raises a clay pyramid on an axis of plazas and buries serpentine pavements and imported jade beneath them.

anchors.title: Paddy rice crosses to northern Kyushu
anchors.summary: Migrants from the Korean peninsula bring wet-rice fields, bronze, and new pottery to western Japan, beginning the Yayoi transformation.

anchors.title: Villanovan villages gather into towns in Etruria
anchors.summary: Iron-using communities in central Italy leave scattered hamlets for large plateau settlements that grow into the Etruscan cities.

anchors.title: Ashurnasirpal II opens his capital at Kalhu
anchors.summary: The new palace at Nimrud is dedicated with a feast for tens of thousands and lined with reliefs that state plainly what Assyria does to cities that resist.

anchors.title: A Kushite kingdom forms at Napata
anchors.summary: Rulers buried at el-Kurru below the holy mountain build a state on Nubian gold and Egyptian cult, and their descendants will rule Egypt itself.

anchors.title: The Gonghe regency begins the dated record
anchors.summary: Revolt drives King Li from the Zhou capital, and the years of the interim government are the first in Chinese history that can be dated exactly.

anchors.title: King Xuan campaigns to restore Zhou authority
anchors.summary: Zhou armies push back the Xianyun in the northwest and lean on the eastern vassals, buying the dynasty two more generations of nominal command.

anchors.title: Tyre's colonists found Carthage
anchors.summary: Tradition dates a Phoenician settlement on the Tunisian shore that grows into the western Mediterranean's dominant trading and naval power.

anchors.title: Aramaic becomes the Near East's common tongue
anchors.summary: Assyrian deportations and caravan trade spread an alphabetic language that clerks and merchants from Egypt to Iran can all read, whatever their king writes in.

anchors.title: Iron tools open the Ganges plain
anchors.summary: Iron axes and ploughshares let farmers clear wet forest and break heavy soil, and the surplus gathers into the subcontinent's second wave of cities.

anchors.title: Greeks add vowels to the Phoenician alphabet
anchors.summary: Unneeded consonant signs are repurposed to write vowels, giving Greek a script that records speech closely enough for verse, law, and accounts alike.

anchors.title: La Venta leads the Olmec heartland
anchors.summary: A center of earthen pyramids and buried jade offerings organizes the Gulf lowlands and sends its carving style inland with the trade in obsidian and stone.

anchors.title: First recorded Olympic games
anchors.summary: Greek cities begin counting years by a shared festival, a calendar of rivals.

anchors.title: The Western Zhou capital falls
anchors.summary: Invaders sack Haojing and kill the king; the court moves east to Luoyi keeping the title while real power passes to the states, and the Spring and Autumn era begins.

anchors.title: Traditional founding of Rome
anchors.summary: A hill town on the Tiber begins the accumulation that will end as the Mediterranean's landlord.

anchors.title: Hallstatt chiefs trade Alpine salt
anchors.summary: Salt cut from Austrian mountains buys imported bronze and southern goods for chieftains whose four-wheeled wagon burials mark the first recognizable Celtic elite.

anchors.title: The Homeric epics are written down
anchors.summary: Oral hexameter about Troy is fixed in the new alphabet, giving scattered Greek cities a shared canon to quote, teach, and argue with for a thousand years.

anchors.title: Paracas culture emerges on Peru's south coast
anchors.summary: Desert communities develop a ceramic and weaving tradition, and a surgical practice of skull trepanation, that the dry sand will preserve for two millennia.

anchors.title: Tiglath-Pileser III remakes Assyria
anchors.summary: A standing army, salaried governors, and the mass deportation of conquered peoples turn a raiding kingdom into an administered empire that others will copy.

anchors.title: Corinth founds Syracuse
anchors.summary: Land-hungry Greek cities plant settlements from Sicily to the Black Sea, each carrying its mother city's cults, script, and quarrels to a new coast.

anchors.title: Sparta conquers Messenia
anchors.summary: Sparta seizes its neighbour's farmland and binds the population as helots; the permanent risk of revolt shapes every Spartan institution that follows.

anchors.title: Kushite kings take the Egyptian throne
anchors.summary: Piye's armies march north from Napata and a Nubian dynasty rules Egypt for six decades, restoring old temples and old titles as the warrant for its claim.

anchors.title: Samaria falls to Assyria
anchors.summary: The northern kingdom of Israel ends in siege and deportation, its people resettled across the empire; Judah survives alone and remembers.

anchors.title: Etruscan cities organize central Italy
anchors.summary: Federated towns work Tuscan iron and copper, take the alphabet from Greek traders, and pass their drainage engineering and their augury to a small town on the Tiber.

anchors.title: Scythian riders control the Pontic steppe
anchors.summary: Mounted archers dominate the grasslands north of the Black Sea, raiding as far as Assyria and, as Greek colonies appear on their coast, selling grain and slaves to them.

anchors.title: The early Upanishads are composed
anchors.summary: Forest dialogues turn Vedic religion from sacrifice toward inquiry into the self, and set the questions Indian philosophy will argue over for millennia.

anchors.title: Guan Zhong reforms the state of Qi
anchors.summary: Salt and iron monopolies and a registered population fund the army that makes Duke Huan the first hegemon, and rank among the states starts tracking revenue.

anchors.title: Ashurbanipal collects a library at Nineveh
anchors.summary: The Assyrian king has scribes copy omens, epics, and medical texts onto tablets; the fired clay outlasts his empire by two and a half thousand years.

anchors.title: Assyrian armies sack Thebes
anchors.summary: Ashurbanipal's troops strip Egypt's southern capital of its treasure and its Kushite garrison, ending Nubian rule on the lower Nile.

anchors.title: Psamtik I reunifies Egypt
anchors.summary: A vassal at Sais outlives his Assyrian sponsors, takes Thebes without a battle, and opens the Delta to Greek mercenaries and traders on his own terms.

anchors.title: Carthage plants a colony of its own on Ibiza
anchors.summary: With Tyre besieged and taxed by eastern empires, its African daughter city begins founding settlements on its own account and inherits the Phoenician trade of the west.

anchors.title: The hoplite phalanx becomes the Greek norm
anchors.summary: Massed spearmen who buy their own bronze make ordinary farmers decisive in battle, and cities that need them find it hard to deny them a voice.

anchors.title: Phoenician traders work Iberian silver
anchors.summary: Tyre's colonies in the far west buy the silver of Tartessos with oil, cloth, and credit, tying southern Iberia into an eastern Mediterranean market.

anchors.title: Nineveh falls to Medes and Babylonians
anchors.summary: An allied siege destroys the Assyrian capital, and the state that invented imperial administration is gone within three years, its provinces divided by the victors.

anchors.title: Lydia mints the first coins
anchors.summary: Stamped electrum turns trust in metal into trust in the stamp; markets speed up accordingly.

anchors.title: Nebuchadnezzar breaks Egypt at Carchemish
anchors.summary: Babylon's crown prince destroys the Egyptian army in northern Syria and inherits the whole Assyrian west, the small kingdoms of the Levant included.

anchors.title: The Heuneburg becomes a walled town
anchors.summary: A hillfort on the upper Danube is rebuilt with a Mediterranean-style mudbrick wall and houses thousands, the first settlement of town scale north of the Alps.

anchors.title: Sixteen kingdoms take shape in northern India
anchors.summary: Tribal territories harden into rival monarchies and republics with walled capitals and steady revenue, and the competition among them will end with Magadha on top.

anchors.title: Necho II sends a fleet around Africa
anchors.summary: Herodotus records that Phoenician crews hired by the pharaoh sailed south from the Red Sea and came back through the Pillars of Heracles in the third year.

anchors.title: Zoroastrian teaching spreads in Iran
anchors.summary: Hymns ascribed to Zarathushtra set one wise creator against the lie and make each person's choice between them the hinge of the world, a frame later creeds borrow.

anchors.title: Lu taxes fields by area
anchors.summary: The state of Lu begins assessing every plot rather than the old communal allotment, an admission on the record that private landholding has already replaced it.

anchors.title: Solon cancels Athens's debts
anchors.summary: Debt bondage is abolished and political rights are graded by property rather than birth, defusing a crisis without the tyranny both sides had prepared for.

anchors.title: The Kushite court moves to Meroe
anchors.summary: After an Egyptian raid on Napata the kingdom shifts south to grassland with iron ore and rain-fed grain, and governs the middle Nile from there for nine centuries.

anchors.title: Babylon destroys Jerusalem
anchors.summary: The temple is burned and Judah's elite deported to Babylon, where exile turns a temple cult into a portable religion of text, law, and memory.

anchors.title: Thales is credited with predicting a solar eclipse
anchors.summary: A Milesian accounts for the sky by causes instead of gods, and the Ionian habit of asking what things are made of hardens into a tradition with successors.

anchors.title: Cyrus overthrows the Medes
anchors.summary: A Persian vassal takes his overlord's capital and army intact, and begins the twenty years of conquest that will assemble the largest empire yet governed.

anchors.title: Cyrus takes Babylon
anchors.summary: The Persian empire assembles the largest state yet seen and governs it with roads, satraps, and tolerance.

anchors.title: Zheng casts its penal code in bronze
anchors.summary: Zichan has the state's punishments inscribed where anyone may read them, and traditionalists object that law the people can see is law the nobles can no longer bend.

anchors.title: Tragedy is staged at the City Dionysia
anchors.summary: Athens adds a contest for tragic drama to its spring festival, and a chorus answered by one speaking actor becomes the city's yearly argument with itself.

anchors.title: Mahavira leaves an ordered Jain community
anchors.summary: The last tirthankara's insistence on non-injury and ascetic vows is carried on by monks, nuns, and lay followers organized to outlast their teacher.

anchors.title: Persia conquers Egypt
anchors.summary: Cambyses beats the Saite army at Pelusium and Egypt becomes a satrapy, taxed, garrisoned, and answerable to a court a thousand miles east.

anchors.title: Darius seizes the Persian throne
anchors.summary: After a year of revolts he carves his account of them on a cliff at Behistun in three languages, then rebuilds the empire as taxed satrapies with a royal road between them.

anchors.title: Rome expels its kings
anchors.summary: The monarchy gives way to two consuls elected for a year and a senate of former magistrates, an arrangement built against tyranny that will govern for four centuries.

anchors.title: Cleisthenes reforms Athens
anchors.summary: Athenian citizenship is rewired around neighborhoods instead of clans; the demos becomes an institution.

anchors.title: The Art of War treats war as calculation
anchors.summary: A treatise ascribed to Sun Wu argues that terrain, supply, and deception settle battles before they are joined, and becomes required reading for Chinese commanders.

anchors.title: Axial Age teachers reframe ethics across Eurasia
anchors.summary: Within a few generations Greek philosophers, Hebrew prophets, Indian renouncers, and Chinese masters each move authority from inherited ritual toward argued principle.

anchors.title: The Buddha teaches in the Ganges valley
anchors.summary: A renouncer's answer to suffering begins its long migration across Asia.

anchors.title: Teachings attributed to Laozi take shape
anchors.summary: The sayings later gathered as the Daodejing counsel yielding, restraint, and rule by not interfering, and give China a lasting counterweight to Confucian activism.

anchors.title: Monte Alban is founded above Oaxaca
anchors.summary: Zapotec communities level a hilltop and build a shared capital whose carved slabs carry glyphs and dates, the earliest writing and the first state-scale center in the highlands.

anchors.title: Nok culture smelts iron in West Africa
anchors.summary: Furnaces south of the Sahara work iron early and independently; the technology spreads with Bantu-speaking farmers.

anchors.title: Punch-marked silver circulates in northern India
anchors.summary: Guilds and kingdoms stamp weighed silver with their own marks, and the Ganges cities acquire money that does not depend on any single ruler's promise.

anchors.title: The Ionian cities revolt against Persia
anchors.summary: Greek cities on the Anatolian coast rise against their satraps and burn Sardis with Athenian help, and Darius acquires a reason to look west.

anchors.title: Confucius wanders between courts
anchors.summary: A failed office-seeker's teachings on ritual and duty become East Asia's administrative ethic.

anchors.title: Athens wins at Marathon
anchors.summary: A citizen militia defeats a Persian landing force on its own beach, and Athens gains a founding story about what free men in ranks can do.

anchors.title: The first Buddhist council meets at Rajagriha
anchors.summary: Monks recite and agree the Buddha's discourses and monastic rules soon after his death, fixing by trained memory what will only be written down centuries later.

anchors.title: Syracuse defeats Carthage at Himera
anchors.summary: Gelon's victory checks Carthaginian expansion in Sicily for seventy years and funds a building programme that makes Syracuse the richest city in the Greek west.

anchors.title: Greek fleets win at Salamis
anchors.summary: The Persian advance into the Aegean stalls in a strait; the Greek experiment keeps its independence.

anchors.title: The pass at Thermopylae is held and lost
anchors.summary: A small Greek force delays the Persian army for three days and is destroyed once the pass is turned, buying time for the fleet and a story for everyone afterwards.

anchors.title: Plataea ends the Persian invasion
anchors.summary: A combined Greek army destroys the Persian land force in Boeotia, and the attempt on the mainland is over within a year of the sea fight at Salamis.

anchors.title: The Delian League becomes an Athenian empire
anchors.summary: Allied cities pool ships and money against Persia, then discover that the treasury has moved to Athens and that leaving the alliance is not permitted.

anchors.title: Three families divide the state of Jin
anchors.summary: The strongest of the Zhou states is carved up by its own ministerial houses, and the survivors stop pretending that hegemony restrains anyone.

anchors.title: La Tene metalwork spreads across Celtic Europe
anchors.summary: A curvilinear style travels with warriors, smiths, and traders from the Danube to Ireland, marking a Celtic world with shared tastes and no shared state.

anchors.title: Rome publishes the Twelve Tables
anchors.summary: Plebeian pressure forces the city's customary law onto public tablets, so that a magistrate's judgement can be checked against a text any citizen may read.

anchors.title: The Peloponnesian war begins
anchors.summary: Athens and Sparta spend a generation demonstrating how rich democracies and disciplined oligarchies exhaust each other.

anchors.title: Plague strikes besieged Athens
anchors.summary: An epidemic runs through a city packed behind its own walls and kills perhaps a quarter of the population, Pericles among them, while the war continues outside.

anchors.title: Athens surrenders to Sparta
anchors.summary: Twenty-seven years of war end with the fleet gone, the long walls pulled down, and the Aegean empire dismantled; the victors quarrel over the pieces within a decade.

anchors.title: The Warring States period opens
anchors.summary: The Zhou king recognizes Han, Wei, and Zhao as states in their own right, conceding that the old order is finished and that seven powers now compete for all of it.

anchors.title: Greek mercenaries march home from Babylonia
anchors.summary: Hired by a failed claimant to the Persian throne, ten thousand infantry fight their way to the Black Sea and demonstrate how thin the empire's centre has become.

anchors.title: Iron-using farmers settle Africa's Great Lakes
anchors.summary: Bantu-speaking cultivators with iron tools and cereals occupy the lakes region, absorbing or displacing foraging communities and carrying both language and metallurgy south.

anchors.title: Gauls sack Rome
anchors.summary: A Senonian warband breaks the legions at the Allia and burns the city; Rome pays them off, builds a stone circuit wall, and keeps the grudge for centuries.

anchors.title: Plato founds the Academy
anchors.summary: A school in an olive grove outside Athens teaches geometry and dialectic as training for rule, and goes on teaching in one form or another for centuries.

anchors.title: Shang Yang remakes Qin by statute
anchors.summary: Rank awarded for enemies killed, households registered in mutual-liability groups, and hereditary privilege cancelled turn a frontier state into the most efficient army in China.

anchors.title: Panini codifies the grammar of Sanskrit
anchors.summary: Some four thousand ordered rules describe a language precisely enough to generate it; the analysis fixes literary Sanskrit and is still studied by linguists.

anchors.title: Philip II wins at Chaeronea
anchors.summary: Macedonian pikes break the Theban and Athenian levies in one morning; the Greek cities keep their walls and lose their foreign policy.

anchors.title: Aristotle founds the Lyceum
anchors.summary: A school that collects constitutions, dissects animals, and sorts inquiry into named disciplines gives later scholarship both its categories and its habits.

anchors.title: Alexander overthrows Persia at Gaugamela
anchors.summary: A Macedonian army ends the Achaemenid order; Greek becomes the administrative language from the Nile to the Indus.

anchors.title: Alexandria is founded on the Nile delta
anchors.summary: A gridded port laid out on the conqueror's orders at the delta's western edge becomes, within a century, the largest city and busiest harbour in the Greek world.

anchors.title: Alexander dies at Babylon
anchors.summary: A king of thirty-two leaves no viable heir; his generals divide the conquest between them and spend the next forty years fighting over the pieces.

anchors.title: Chandragupta founds the Maurya empire
anchors.summary: Magadha's throne is taken by a commander who then pushes the Macedonian garrisons back beyond the Indus; most of the subcontinent comes under one administration.

anchors.title: Mencius argues for benevolent government
anchors.summary: The Confucian teacher tells warring kings that a ruler who starves his people forfeits the mandate; the claim becomes orthodoxy and a standing licence to rebel.

anchors.title: Rome builds its first highway and aqueduct
anchors.summary: Appius Claudius drives a paved road toward Capua and channels water into the city in the same censorship; Roman power acquires its characteristic public works.

anchors.title: Ptolemy takes the Egyptian crown
anchors.summary: Alexander's general declares himself king and governs the Nile through Greek officials laid over an old temple bureaucracy; his house rules Egypt for nearly three centuries.

anchors.title: Seleucus trades the Indus lands for elephants
anchors.summary: The Macedonian claimant cedes the eastern provinces to Chandragupta for five hundred war elephants and sends an envoy to Pataliputra who writes up what he sees.

anchors.title: Ipsus fixes the successor kingdoms
anchors.summary: The last attempt to hold Alexander's empire whole fails in Phrygia; the conquest is partitioned for good and the Hellenistic world settles into competing kingdoms.

anchors.title: Seleucus plants Antioch and Seleucia
anchors.summary: Two Greek capitals, one on the Orontes and one on the Tigris, anchor a realm governed through colonists, garrisons, and coined silver rather than old temple cities.

anchors.title: The Arthashastra sets out statecraft
anchors.summary: A manual on taxes, spies, famine reserves, and war advises rulers without moralizing; India acquires a systematic literature of administration.

anchors.title: Euclid compiles the Elements
anchors.summary: Definitions, postulates, and proofs in strict order turn scattered geometry into a system; the book remains a working textbook for over two thousand years.

anchors.title: Wet-rice farming opens the Yayoi period
anchors.summary: Paddy agriculture, bronze, and iron cross from the mainland into Kyushu; population climbs, storehouses fill, and the archipelago's first ranked chiefdoms appear.

anchors.title: The Library of Alexandria is endowed
anchors.summary: The Ptolemies pay scholars to collect, copy, and correct everything written in Greek, knowledge as state project.

anchors.title: Pyrrhus invades Italy
anchors.summary: The Epirote king beats Roman armies twice at a cost he cannot replace and sails home; the Greek cities of the south pass to Rome within a decade.

anchors.title: Celtic settlers seize central Anatolia
anchors.summary: Warbands ferried across the straits as mercenaries take the highlands and hold them for centuries as Galatia, taxing the Greek cities for quiet.

anchors.title: Meroe smelts iron on the middle Nile
anchors.summary: Kushite furnaces leave slag mounds around the royal city; iron tools and weapons underwrite a kingdom trading with Egypt, the Red Sea, and the African interior.

anchors.title: The First Punic War begins
anchors.summary: A quarrel over Messina draws Rome into twenty-three years of naval war with Carthage; Rome learns to build fleets and takes Sicily as its first province.

anchors.title: Li Bing builds the Dujiangyan works
anchors.summary: A dividing weir and spillway on the Min river control floods and irrigate the Chengdu plain without a dam; the system still waters those fields, and Qin gains a granary.

anchors.title: Ashoka carves his edicts
anchors.summary: After the slaughter at Kalinga, the Mauryan emperor advertises remorse and dharma on pillars across India.

anchors.title: El Mirador raises the first great Maya cities
anchors.summary: Preclassic builders in the Peten stack platforms bigger in volume than anything later Maya dynasties raise, and link swamp-edge centres with causeways above the wet ground.

anchors.title: Hebrew scripture is translated into Greek
anchors.summary: Alexandria's Jewish community renders its law into Greek; the text travels wherever Greek is read and later gives Christian preaching its scriptures ready-made.

anchors.title: Buddhism reaches Sri Lanka
anchors.summary: A mission sent from Ashoka's court converts the king at Anuradhapura; the island becomes keeper of the Pali canon and a base for later teaching eastward.

anchors.title: Arsaces founds the Parthian kingdom
anchors.summary: A steppe chief takes the satrapy of Parthia from the Seleucids; his house will rule Iran for nearly five centuries and hold Rome at the Euphrates.

anchors.title: Eratosthenes measures the Earth
anchors.summary: Shadow angles at Alexandria and Syene plus a surveyed distance between them yield a circumference within a few percent of the true figure.

anchors.title: Qin unifies China
anchors.summary: Weights, measures, axle widths, and script are standardized at sword-point; the imperial template is set.

anchors.title: Hannibal crosses the Alps
anchors.summary: A Carthaginian army with elephants enters Italy from the north, losing thousands on the passes, and then wins in the peninsula for fifteen years without taking Rome.

anchors.title: Hannibal destroys a Roman army at Cannae
anchors.summary: Rome loses perhaps fifty thousand men in an afternoon and, decisively, declines to negotiate.

anchors.title: Qin links the northern walls
anchors.summary: Conscripts and convicts join existing frontier ramparts into one line against the steppe; the labour and grain it consumes help exhaust the dynasty that ordered it.

anchors.title: Qin burns the books
anchors.summary: Li Si has privately held odes, documents, and rival philosophies destroyed and their defenders punished; much of the older literature survives only by memory or concealment.

anchors.title: Syracuse falls and Archimedes is killed
anchors.summary: Roman troops storm the city after a two-year siege held off by his engines; a soldier kills the mathematician against orders, and his manuscripts scatter.

anchors.title: Modu unites the Xiongnu
anchors.summary: The steppe north of China consolidates under one chanyu; for the first time a nomad confederation can meet the Chinese state as an equal power.

anchors.title: Liu Bang founds the Han dynasty
anchors.summary: A village officer turned rebel takes the throne, keeps Qin's administrative machinery, and repeals its harshest penalties; the compromise governs China for four centuries.

anchors.title: Scipio defeats Hannibal at Zama
anchors.summary: Carthage surrenders its fleet, its Spanish silver, and its right to make war; Rome is left the only great power in the western Mediterranean.

anchors.title: Dong Son bronze drums circulate by sea
anchors.summary: Casters in the Red River valley turn out large decorated drums that reach islands a thousand miles away, evidence of a connected maritime world before Indian influence arrives.

anchors.title: The Garamantes farm the central Sahara
anchors.summary: Tunnels cut into fossil aquifers water grain and dates in the Fezzan, supporting walled towns that broker traffic between the Mediterranean coast and the Sahel.

anchors.title: Paracas weavers wrap their dead in embroidery
anchors.summary: Workshops on the Peruvian south coast produce burial cloth of extraordinary dyed needlework; on this coast textiles, not metal or script, carry rank and record.

anchors.title: Han buys peace from the Xiongnu
anchors.summary: After the emperor is trapped at Baideng, the court sends silk, grain, and a princess north each year; tribute stands in for a war the new dynasty cannot yet win.

anchors.title: Memphis priests decree honours for Ptolemy V
anchors.summary: The text is cut in hieroglyphic, demotic, and Greek and set up in the temples; one surviving copy will let scholars read Egyptian again two thousand years later.

anchors.title: The Maurya empire ends in a coup
anchors.summary: The general Pushyamitra kills the last Mauryan king at a parade and founds the Shunga dynasty; north India returns to a field of competing kingdoms.

anchors.title: Rome ends the Macedonian kingdom at Pydna
anchors.summary: The legion beats the phalanx decisively; Macedon is broken into four republics and the Greek states begin taking their instructions from the Senate.

anchors.title: The Maccabean revolt begins
anchors.summary: Seleucid attempts to suppress temple worship in Jerusalem provoke a rising that within twenty-five years wins an independent Jewish state.

anchors.title: Menander rules an Indo-Greek kingdom
anchors.summary: A Greek king in the Punjab strikes bilingual coin and is remembered as the questioner in a Buddhist dialogue; Hellenistic and Indian forms meet in Gandharan workshops.

anchors.title: Celtic oppida become towns
anchors.summary: Fortified hilltop settlements from Bohemia to Gaul strike coin, work iron in quantity, and concentrate trade; temperate Europe has urban centres before Rome arrives.

anchors.title: Carthage is destroyed
anchors.summary: Rome erases its rival and inherits the western Mediterranean's trade whole.

anchors.title: Corinth is destroyed and Greece annexed
anchors.summary: Rome sacks the city, sells its people into slavery, and dissolves the Achaean league; Greek artists, teachers, and looted statuary move to Italian houses.

anchors.title: Parthia takes Mesopotamia
anchors.summary: Mithridates I enters Seleucia and the Seleucid state shrinks back to Syria; the caravan roads between the Mediterranean and inner Asia change masters and tolls.

anchors.title: Han China adopts the Confucian classics
anchors.summary: Emperor Wu establishes chairs for the five classics and staffs an imperial academy from them; a fixed canon becomes the ladder into government and stays one for two millennia.

anchors.title: Tiberius Gracchus is killed in Rome
anchors.summary: A tribune's bill to resettle dispossessed farmers on public land ends with senators clubbing him to death; Roman politics accepts violence as a working method.

anchors.title: Han envoys open the western routes
anchors.summary: Zhang Qian's missions link Chinese silk to Central Asian horses and, eventually, Roman silver.

anchors.title: Gaius Gracchus dies; the grain dole survives
anchors.summary: The younger brother's subsidized grain, colonies, and court reform outlast him, and the Senate's first emergency decree sets the pattern for killing reformers legally.

anchors.title: The Cimbri and Teutones move south
anchors.summary: Migrating peoples from the north destroy several Roman armies over a decade before Marius annihilates them; Italy learns to fear whatever lives beyond the Alps.

anchors.title: Rome goes to war with Jugurtha in Numidia
anchors.summary: A North African king buys senators until the command passes to outsiders; Marius and Sulla make their names, and senatorial corruption becomes a public argument.

anchors.title: Marius opens the legions to the landless
anchors.summary: Recruitment without a property qualification fills the ranks with men who own nothing and look to their general, not the Senate, for land at discharge.

anchors.title: Petra grows rich on the incense road
anchors.summary: Nabataean engineers cut cisterns, dams, and channels into sandstone and tax the caravans carrying frankincense north; water management pays for the monumental tombs.

anchors.title: Tamil kingdoms trade pepper and compile poems
anchors.summary: Chera, Chola, and Pandya ports send pepper and pearls west to Greek and Arab shippers, while their court poets assemble the anthologies that anchor Tamil literature.

anchors.title: Teotihuacan is founded in the valley of Mexico
anchors.summary: Settlers gather at a spring-fed site northeast of the lakes and lay out the grid and platform mounds that will grow into the largest city in the Americas.

anchors.title: Sima Qian completes the Shiji
anchors.summary: A court historian, mutilated as a punishment and kept in office, finishes a history from legend to his own day and fixes the form Chinese historiography will keep.

anchors.title: Sulla marches his army on Rome
anchors.summary: A consul turns his legions against the city to keep a command voted away from him; the precedent, once available, is used again until the Republic is gone.

anchors.title: The slave revolt under Spartacus
anchors.summary: Escaped gladiators raise an army of tens of thousands across Italy; after two years Crassus defeats them and has six thousand crucified along the road to Capua.

anchors.title: Pompey takes Jerusalem
anchors.summary: Having annexed the Seleucid remnant as a province the year before, Pompey storms the temple mount and makes Judaea a client; Rome's frontier now faces Parthia's.

anchors.title: Caesar begins the conquest of Gaul
anchors.summary: Eight years of campaigning kill or enslave a large part of the Gallic population and deliver Rome a wealthy province, along with the veteran army that will take Rome itself.

anchors.title: Roman ships reach Britain
anchors.summary: Two short campaigns win hostages and promises of tribute but no ground; Britain enters the written record and stays outside the empire for another century.

anchors.title: Parthian cavalry destroys Crassus at Carrhae
anchors.summary: Horse archers and armoured lancers wreck seven legions on the Mesopotamian plain and take their standards; Rome's expansion eastward halts at the Euphrates.

anchors.title: Vercingetorix surrenders at Alesia
anchors.summary: A double ring of Roman siege works holds off the besieged town and the relief army at once; organized Gallic resistance ends and Latin starts displacing Gaulish.

anchors.title: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
anchors.summary: A proconsul brings a legion into Italy rather than lay down his command and face prosecution; the civil war that follows finishes the Republic he says he is defending.

anchors.title: Fire reaches the Library of Alexandria
anchors.summary: During Caesar's Alexandrian war, fire spreads from the docks and part of the library's holdings burn.

anchors.title: The Julian calendar is adopted
anchors.summary: Caesar's astronomers give Rome a 365-day year with a leap day after one year of 445 days to clear the drift; the reckoning survives, lightly corrected, to the present.

anchors.title: Caesar is assassinated
anchors.summary: The Republic's defenders kill the dictator and get, within twenty years, a permanent monarchy anyway.

anchors.title: Octavian wins at Actium
anchors.summary: Agrippa's fleet pins Antony and Cleopatra off the Greek coast and their army melts away; the last rival power block is gone and one man holds every province.

anchors.title: Rome annexes Egypt
anchors.summary: Cleopatra's death ends the Ptolemies and puts the Nile's grain under the emperor's personal control; Rome's bread supply becomes a strategic asset and a political lever.

anchors.title: Augustus founds the principate
anchors.summary: Rome's civil wars end in an emperor who insists he is merely first citizen; the fiction holds for centuries.

anchors.title: Arminius destroys three legions at Teutoburg
anchors.summary: Three Roman legions are annihilated in a German forest by allied tribes under a Roman-trained officer, and the northern frontier settles on the Rhine rather than the Elbe.

anchors.title: Wang Mang usurps the Han throne
anchors.summary: A regent declares the Xin dynasty and decrees land redistribution and currency reform; flood, famine, and revolt undo the program and its author within fifteen years.

anchors.title: Augustus dies and Tiberius succeeds
anchors.summary: The first emperor dies in his bed after forty years in power, and the office passes to his stepson without civil war; the principate proves it can be inherited.

anchors.title: Liu Xiu restores the Han at Luoyang
anchors.summary: After a decade of civil war a Han claimant refounds the dynasty in a new eastern capital, ruling for nearly two centuries in partnership with the great landholding families.

anchors.title: Jesus of Nazareth is crucified in Jerusalem
anchors.summary: A Galilean teacher is executed by Roman authority during Passover, and his followers' claims about what happened next become the seed of a new religion.

anchors.title: Kujula Kadphises unites the Kushan tribes
anchors.summary: Five Yuezhi chiefdoms are welded into one kingdom that will hold the passes between India, Iran, and the caravan roads of Central Asia.

anchors.title: Claudius invades Britain
anchors.summary: Four legions cross the Channel and take the southeast of the island, beginning nearly four centuries of Roman provincial rule in Britain.

anchors.title: The Jerusalem council admits gentile converts
anchors.summary: The apostles agree that non-Jewish believers need not keep the whole Mosaic law, and the movement's future becomes Greek-speaking, urban, and Mediterranean-wide.

anchors.title: Roman ships reach the Malabar pepper ports
anchors.summary: Monsoon sailing carries fleets from Egypt to Muziris and back within a season, trading Roman gold for pepper, gems, and cotton in volumes that alarm Roman moralists.

anchors.title: Buddhism reaches the Han court
anchors.summary: Tradition dates the first monks and sutras at Luoyang to an imperial embassy, beginning the long work of rendering an Indian religion into Chinese.

anchors.title: Titus destroys the Second Temple
anchors.summary: Rome ends the Jewish revolt by storming Jerusalem and burning the Temple, and Judaism reorganizes around law, text, and synagogue instead of sacrifice.

anchors.title: Pliny publishes the Natural History
anchors.summary: Thirty-seven books compile what Rome believed about minerals, plants, medicine, and art, and the encyclopedia becomes a genre Europe copies for a thousand years.

anchors.title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii and Herculaneum
anchors.summary: Ash fall and pyroclastic surges bury two Campanian towns within a day, killing thousands and sealing their streets, shops, and graffiti for later excavation.

anchors.title: The Colosseum opens in Rome
anchors.summary: The Flavians fund an arena for tens of thousands out of the spoils of Judaea, making sponsored games a permanent instrument of imperial politics.

anchors.title: The gospels are set down in Greek
anchors.summary: Four narrative accounts of Jesus circulate within living memory of the events, fixing an oral movement in portable text that can travel the trade routes.

anchors.title: Ban Chao secures the Western Regions
anchors.summary: Han arms and alliances restore control of the Tarim oases, keeping the caravan roads toward Kushan and Parthian markets open for a generation.

anchors.title: Hopewell earthworks anchor a wide exchange
anchors.summary: Ohio valley communities raise banked geometric enclosures and bury obsidian, copper, and marine shell drawn from half a continent.

anchors.title: Meroe works iron on the middle Nile
anchors.summary: The Kushite capital smelts iron in quantity and trades gold, ivory, and cattle north to Rome, keeping its accounts in a Meroitic script still only partly read.

anchors.title: The Nazca lines are traced in the desert
anchors.summary: Coastal communities clear dark stone from the pampa to expose straight lines running for kilometers and animal figures hundreds of meters across, apparently laid out to be walked in ritual.

anchors.title: Cai Lun standardizes papermaking
anchors.summary: Rags and bark become a writing surface cheap enough for bureaucracy at scale.

anchors.title: Trajan's harbor opens at Portus
anchors.summary: A hexagonal artificial basin at the Tiber mouth lets the Egyptian grain fleet unload in almost any weather, securing the bread supply of a million-person city.

anchors.title: Rome reaches its greatest extent
anchors.summary: Trajan's Parthian campaign carries Roman arms to the Persian Gulf, and his successor gives the new eastern provinces up within a year of inheriting them.

anchors.title: Gautamiputra Satakarni restores Satavahana power
anchors.summary: The Deccan king drives back the Western Satraps and taxes the routes crossing India between the Arabian Sea ports and the Bay of Bengal.

anchors.title: Hadrian's Wall is begun across Britain
anchors.summary: Eighty Roman miles of stone, ditch, and garrisoned fort mark a frontier in the north, and the empire commits to holding a line rather than advancing.

anchors.title: The Pantheon's concrete dome is completed
anchors.summary: Roman concrete graded from heavy basalt to light pumice spans forty-three meters without reinforcement, and no wider dome is built anywhere for thirteen centuries.

anchors.title: Kanishka rules the Kushan empire at its height
anchors.summary: The Kushan court holds territory from Bactria to Mathura, endows Buddhist monasteries, and mints a gold coinage struck to the weight of the Roman aureus.

anchors.title: Hadrian fixes the praetor's edict
anchors.summary: The annually reissued magistrate's edict is codified once and for good, and Roman private law passes from elected officials to professional jurists.

anchors.title: The Bar Kokhba revolt
anchors.summary: A three-year Jewish rising against Rome ends in mass death and depopulation, with Jews barred from Jerusalem and the province renamed Syria Palaestina.

anchors.title: Zhang Heng builds a seismoscope
anchors.summary: A bronze vessel at the Han court drops a ball toward the bearing of a distant earthquake, reporting the shock days before any courier can arrive.

anchors.title: The Way of the Celestial Masters is founded
anchors.summary: Zhang Daoling's revelation organizes households into parishes with priests, registers, and tithes, giving Daoism an institutional church.

anchors.title: The Garamantes irrigate the central Sahara
anchors.summary: Kilometers of underground channels tap fossil water beneath the Fezzan, supporting towns, cereal farming, and caravan traffic across a desert otherwise closed.

anchors.title: Ptolemy compiles the Almagest
anchors.summary: An Alexandrian astronomer fixes an Earth-centered model with tables accurate enough to serve astronomers in three religions for fourteen centuries.

anchors.title: Funan's port at Oc Eo links two ocean trades
anchors.summary: A canal-served harbor on the Mekong delta handles Indian, Chinese, and Mediterranean goods, among them a medallion struck for Antoninus Pius.

anchors.title: Gaius writes the Institutes
anchors.summary: A teaching manual sorts Roman law into persons, things, and actions, a scheme that still organizes civil codes on four continents.

anchors.title: The Antonine plague sweeps the Roman world
anchors.summary: Soldiers returning from the east carry a pandemic that hollows cities and armies for a generation.

anchors.title: Germanic peoples break the Danube frontier
anchors.summary: Marcomanni and Quadi cross into the approaches to Italy, and Rome spends a decade and much of its treasury pushing them back behind the river.

anchors.title: Galen systematizes classical medicine
anchors.summary: A physician to gladiators and emperors builds anatomy, pharmacy, and humoral theory into a corpus that governs medicine in Europe and Islam for fourteen centuries.

anchors.title: Marcus Aurelius keeps the Meditations
anchors.summary: An emperor campaigning on the Danube writes Stoic notes to himself that were never meant for readers and have not been out of circulation since.

anchors.title: Buddhist sutras are translated into Chinese
anchors.summary: A Kushan monk at Luoyang renders Mahayana texts into a language with no vocabulary for their ideas, giving Chinese Buddhism its first scriptures of the great vehicle.

anchors.title: The Yellow Turban rebellion
anchors.summary: A Daoist healing movement raises hundreds of thousands against the Han, and suppressing it transfers real power to the regional generals who do the work.

anchors.title: Farming communities reach southern Africa
anchors.summary: Iron tools, cattle, and cereal cultivation arrive south of the Limpopo with Bantu-speaking migrants, reworking the subcontinent's languages and economy.

anchors.title: Nagarjuna argues the emptiness doctrine
anchors.summary: A southern Indian monk's dialectic denies that anything holds independent existence, founding a school that will shape Buddhist thought from Tibet to Japan.

anchors.title: Cao Cao is checked at Red Cliffs
anchors.summary: A defeat on the Yangtze stops the north from reuniting China by force, and the country settles into the three-way division that follows.

anchors.title: Caracalla extends citizenship to the empire
anchors.summary: Nearly every free inhabitant becomes a Roman citizen, widening the inheritance tax base and emptying an old legal distinction of most of its meaning.

anchors.title: The Han dynasty falls
anchors.summary: China fractures into three kingdoms; four centuries of division begin.

anchors.title: Ardashir overthrows the Parthian king
anchors.summary: A Persian vassal defeats his Arsacid overlord in battle and founds a centralized Sasanian state with a Zoroastrian priesthood as its establishment.

anchors.title: The crisis of the third century begins
anchors.summary: The murder of Severus Alexander opens fifty years of usurpation, invasion, and silver debasement that nearly break the Roman empire into pieces.

anchors.title: Mani begins preaching in Persia
anchors.summary: A prophet combining Christian, Zoroastrian, and Buddhist material founds a missionary faith with its own scriptures that will reach Roman Africa and China alike.

anchors.title: The Plague of Cyprian spreads through the empire
anchors.summary: A second pandemic runs through the Roman world for more than a decade, thinning armies and taxpayers at the worst moment of the political crisis.

anchors.title: Aksum dominates Red Sea trade
anchors.summary: An Ethiopian kingdom mints its own gold and brokers between Rome and India.

anchors.title: Decius orders universal sacrifice
anchors.summary: Every inhabitant must sacrifice to the gods and carry a certificate proving it, and the first empire-wide persecution splits Christian communities over who complied.

anchors.title: A Moche lord is buried at Sipan
anchors.summary: A north-coast ruler goes into the ground with gold, turquoise, and attendants, evidence of hereditary lordship and specialist metalwork on the Peruvian coast.

anchors.title: Goths kill a Roman emperor at Abritus
anchors.summary: Decius dies fighting in the marshes of Moesia, the first Roman emperor killed by a foreign enemy, and Gothic raiding becomes an annual expectation.

anchors.title: Shapur captures the emperor Valerian
anchors.summary: A Roman emperor is taken alive near Edessa and dies in Persian captivity, and Sasanian rock reliefs advertise the humiliation for centuries.

anchors.title: Antony withdraws to the Egyptian desert
anchors.summary: An Egyptian layman gives away his land and settles alone beyond the cultivated valley, and the ascetic life he models becomes Christian monasticism.

anchors.title: Aurelian walls the city of Rome
anchors.summary: Nineteen kilometers of brick-faced wall go up around a capital that had gone three centuries without needing any defenses of its own.

anchors.title: Jin reunifies China
anchors.summary: The conquest of Wu ends sixty years of division, and the reunion holds for one generation before civil war among the princes and invasion from the north undo it.

anchors.title: Tikal raises a Long Count dated stela
anchors.summary: The earliest firmly dated monument in the Maya lowlands opens the Classic record, as dynasties begin publishing their reigns and ancestries in carved stone.

anchors.title: Diocletian divides the empire in four
anchors.summary: Two senior and two junior emperors take charge of separate provinces, armies, and successions, stabilizing the state and roughly doubling its bureaucracy.

anchors.title: Diocletian caps prices across the empire
anchors.summary: An edict fixes maximum prices and wages for a thousand goods to halt debasement-driven inflation; merchants withhold stock instead, and the ceilings quietly lapse.

anchors.title: Liu Yuan proclaims a Han restoration in the north
anchors.summary: A Xiongnu chieftain claims the Han mandate against the Jin, and north China breaks into the succession of short-lived states later called the Sixteen Kingdoms.

anchors.title: Constantine backs Christianity
anchors.summary: An emperor's battlefield vow moves a persecuted sect toward establishment.

anchors.title: The Edict of Milan legalizes Christian worship
anchors.summary: Constantine and Licinius agree to restore confiscated churches and tolerate all cults; persecution ends as imperial policy and the church begins accumulating property.

anchors.title: The Jin court re-establishes itself at Jiankang
anchors.summary: Refugee northern aristocrats rebuild the dynasty south of the Yangtze, and the lower Yangtze begins its long rise as China's demographic and economic center.

anchors.title: Chandragupta I founds the Gupta empire
anchors.summary: A Magadhan ruler marries into the Licchavi line and dates a new era from his accession; north India acquires the dynasty that will pay for its classical age.

anchors.title: The Council of Nicaea defines the creed
anchors.summary: Bishops summoned by an emperor settle the Son's relation to the Father and condemn Arius; doctrine becomes an imperial concern, enforceable by exile.

anchors.title: Constantinople is dedicated
anchors.summary: Rome gets a second capital on the Bosporus, better placed for the empire's money and enemies alike.

anchors.title: Aksum adopts Christianity under Ezana
anchors.summary: The king's coins exchange the crescent and disc for the cross, and Ethiopia begins sixteen centuries of Christian statehood on the Red Sea.

anchors.title: Aksumite armies end the kingdom of Kush
anchors.summary: Ezana's campaign up the Nile leaves Meroe's temples and iron furnaces derelict, ending a Nubian kingdom that had outlasted pharaonic Egypt itself.

anchors.title: Samudragupta records his conquests at Allahabad
anchors.summary: An inscription cut onto an Ashokan pillar lists kings defeated and kings left tributary, mapping a Gupta paramountcy that governs through subordinate courts.

anchors.title: Julian restores the old cults
anchors.summary: The last pagan emperor reopens the temples, revokes clerical privileges, and bars Christians from teaching the classics; his death two years later ends the attempt.

anchors.title: Jovian cedes Nisibis to Persia
anchors.summary: To extract a beaten army from Mesopotamia, a new emperor surrenders five provinces beyond the Tigris and the fortress city that had anchored Rome's eastern frontier for generations.

anchors.title: Buddhism reaches Goguryeo
anchors.summary: A monk arrives from the Former Qin court with images and sutras, beginning the transmission that Korean kingdoms will later carry, with their craftsmen, on to Japan.

anchors.title: The Huns break the Gothic kingdoms
anchors.summary: Mounted archers out of the steppe shatter the Greuthungi and push whole Gothic peoples onto the Danube, where Rome must decide whether to admit them.

anchors.title: Valens is killed at Adrianople
anchors.summary: A Gothic army destroys the eastern field force and kills the emperor commanding it; Rome thereafter settles whole peoples inside the frontier as allied armies rather than as subjects.

anchors.title: Teotihuacan's agents install a new dynasty at Tikal
anchors.summary: Siyaj K'ak' arrives from the west on the day Tikal's king dies, and central Mexican arms, dress, and gods enter Maya royal display for a century.

anchors.title: Nicene Christianity becomes the state religion
anchors.summary: Theodosius orders all subjects to hold the faith of Rome and Alexandria; those who dissent are named heretics and lose the law's protection.

anchors.title: The Eastern Jin hold the Fei river
anchors.summary: A far larger Former Qin army dissolves in retreat and its empire with it; the Yangtze line holds, and China's split into north and south is fixed for two centuries.

anchors.title: The empire is divided between Theodosius' sons
anchors.summary: East and west take separate courts, armies, and treasuries at his death; the halves never again share a ruler, and only one of them survives the next century.

anchors.title: Gupta India's court science flourishes
anchors.summary: Astronomers and mathematicians at Pataliputra work with a decimal notation the world will eventually borrow.

anchors.title: Teotihuacan at its height
anchors.summary: A gridded metropolis of a hundred thousand or more, ruling central Mexico without a named king history remembers.

anchors.title: Wagadu takes shape in the western Sahel
anchors.summary: Soninke rulers south of the Sahara consolidate a polity on regional exchange in grain, iron, cattle, and Sahelian salt; the trans-Saharan gold traffic that will make Ghana rich is still three centuries off.

anchors.title: The Church of the East organizes at Seleucia-Ctesiphon
anchors.summary: A synod held under Sasanian license gives Persia's Christians their own patriarch and hierarchy, a church that will eventually plant bishops as far east as Chang'an.

anchors.title: Alaric sacks Rome
anchors.summary: The city that had not fallen in eight centuries falls in three days; the shock outruns the damage.

anchors.title: Hypatia is killed in Alexandria
anchors.summary: A mathematician and Neoplatonist teacher is dragged from her carriage and murdered by a mob amid the city's factional politics; Alexandria's pagan schools never recover their standing.

anchors.title: Augustine finishes the City of God
anchors.summary: Writing at Hippo after Rome's sack, a bishop separates the earthly city from the heavenly one and hands Latin Christianity a political theology for a world without empire.

anchors.title: Yax K'uk' Mo' founds the Copan dynasty
anchors.summary: A newcomer king establishes a line that will rule the southeastern Maya frontier for sixteen reigns and leave the region's densest run of dated monuments.

anchors.title: Nalanda is founded in Magadha
anchors.summary: Gupta patronage endows a monastic university whose halls and libraries will draw students from China, Korea, and Tibet for seven hundred years.

anchors.title: The Northern Wei unify northern China
anchors.summary: Tuoba armies absorb the last of the Sixteen Kingdoms, and China settles into the two-court balance of the Northern and Southern Dynasties.

anchors.title: The Vandals take Carthage
